title: When Tibetan Meditation Goes Global: A Study of the Adaptation of Bon Religious Practices in the West
author: Mara Lisa Arizaga (quoting Yongdzin Lopon Tenzin Namdak, Khenpo Tenpa Yungdrung, Tenzin Wangyal and Western retreatants)
edition_cited: De Gruyter, Berlin/Boston 2022, open access CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
tradition: Yungdrung Bon Dzogchen (Zhang Zhung Nyengyud; Shenten Dargye Ling, France)
locator_hints: Chapter 9 'Becoming a Bonpo', pp. 155-156: trekchö/thögal and the 'three supports' (space, darkness, sunlight), with a block quotation from Namdak
Chapter 12.5, p. 229 and note 642: number of participants who did dark retreats
search the file for 'Dark Retreat' and 'three supports'
summary: Ethnography of Western Bon practitioners. Its dark-retreat pages report how the practice is framed and run at a European Bon centre: Yongdzin Tenzin Namdak's statement that darkness serves beginners (to clarify and stabilise the mind) and advanced practitioners (to develop thögal visions); the three 'supports' for vision (dark room, sky, sunlight), with his remark that more visions develop in the dark and fewer but clearer ones with sunlight; the forty-nine-day 'Seven Cycles of Clear Light' appended to the Gyalwa Chaktri, one week per session with breathing, visualisation and postures; the requirement of stable trekchö, guidance and physical and mental fitness; the advice to Westerners to begin with retreats of up to seven days; and figures on how many people did short and full retreats. Little description of what was seen.
why_relevant: Carries lineage holders' practical framing of dark retreat (prerequisites, durations, which support yields what kind of vision) in an openly licensed text; testimony on the light itself is thin.

date_evidence.basis: 'Open Access. © 2022 Mara Lisa Arizaga, published by De Gruyter' printed in the text; archive.org/OAPEN metadata date 2022

notes: An academic study, catalogued only for the teacher statements and retreat arrangements it reports. The quoted teacher sources are Namdak 2010 (Masters of the Zhang Zhung Nyengyud), Lowenthal/Wangyal 2003, Yungdrung 2006, Wangyal 2000: follow those for the primary statements. Mentions Tenzin Wangyal's account of his own dark retreat (Wonders of the Natural Mind, 2000 ed., pp. 24-33).
